concept: mongot replication lag, oplog window and index rebuild cost

claims.text: For precomputed collections queried through Search, pace bulk refresh writes and monitor their write volume together with search replication lag; otherwise a refresh burst can increase staleness and potentially force rebuilding. This application to refresh jobs is an inference from the documented bulk-write failure mode. (medium confidence)

Increasing lag is a warning, but small steady-state lag is normal. During initial sync, the replication-lag metric is not meaningful; diagnose build progress, source throughput, and resource pressure instead. (medium confidence)

Repeated initial-sync transitions are not uniquely evidence of an undersized oplog: MongoDB also lists recurring steady-state exceptions, mapping-driven heap exhaustion, and index corruption. Inspect the preceding log error before selecting a remedy. (low confidence)

When mongot falls behind the retained oplog window, it can no longer recover incrementally and performs a full index rebuild. Oplog rollover, slow indexing, and downtime can produce this condition. (high confidence)

Repeated re-sync is not sufficient proof of oplog exhaustion: MongoDB also lists transient steady-state exceptions, mapping-driven heap exhaustion, corruption, and expensive index definitions. Inspect the preceding error and oplog window before choosing a remedy. (high confidence)

Debezium independently documents the same retained-history constraint for its MongoDB change-stream consumer: a purged resume position prevents resumption and can cause an invalid-resume-token failure depending on snapshot.mode. This supports the general CDC constraint, not mongot-specific recovery behavior. (low confidence)

MongoDB warns that some self-managed index builds can take days; Percona repeats this warning rather than supplying an independent benchmark, so days is a possible recovery case rather than a typical duration or SLA. (medium confidence)

For offload designs that refresh an indexed precomputed collection, budget separately for collection-refresh freshness and downstream search-index freshness. This is an architectural inference from asynchronous indexing, rather than a measured end-to-end freshness guarantee. (medium confidence)

A mongot filesystem snapshot can avoid rebuilding only while change-stream history can carry it forward. If the restored snapshot is older than retained history, mongot rebuilds from mongod instead of simply resuming incremental replication. (high confidence)
mongot consumes mongod changes asynchronously through change streams; a successful database write does not imply that the search index already reflects that write. (high confidence)

If mongot falls behind the retained oplog window, incremental synchronization is no longer possible and a full index rebuild is required; existing search data can remain queryable but stale during recovery. (medium confidence)

A filesystem snapshot avoids rebuilding only while its replication position can still be advanced through retained change-stream history. An older snapshot can be immediately queryable yet require rebuilding to regain freshness. (medium confidence)

Oplog headroom and consumer throughput address different risks: a larger retained history gives mongot more time through pauses or write bursts, while additional indexing capacity or fewer expensive indexes addresses sustained inability to keep up. (medium confidence)

The mongot-doctor repository documents a diagnostic report combining change-stream lag, initial-sync activity, oplog window, JVM heap, Lucene merges, and index health. Its heuristic thresholds and claimed amplification factors are not validated rebuild-cost measurements. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Debezium independently documents the underlying MongoDB CDC retention hazard: after an outage, a saved resume position can have aged out of the oplog, and connector recovery depends on snapshot configuration. This corroborates the retention constraint, not mongot-specific rebuild duration or recovery behavior. (low confidence)

Full index rebuilds are computationally expensive and time-consuming; MongoDB documents that some self-managed index builds can take days. This is a possible recovery duration, not a typical or guaranteed rebuild time. (high confidence)

Monitor replication lag against the oplog window and investigate growing lag together with write rate, CPU, and disk I/O. More retained history increases recovery headroom; additional indexing capacity or reduced write bursts addresses the rate imbalance. (high confidence)

MongoDB self-managed monitoring documents mongot_index_stats_indexing_replicationLagMs as a per-index metric in milliseconds. The metric family is absent before an index exists, so absence must not be interpreted as zero lag. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Search can remain available while a stale index rebuilds: Atlas documents stale results during oplog-triggered rebuilds, and restored self-managed snapshots remain queryable during rebuilding. Availability does not establish freshness. (high confidence)

Alibaba Cloud documents that restoring an ApsaraDB instance from backup does not restore search indexes; users must re-enable Search and rebuild them. This is a service-specific recovery rule and must not be generalized to Atlas or filesystem snapshots of mongot. (low confidence)
